The documentation in the new/refactored execs like this https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/issues/357#issuecomment-4167289382 is not standard with the existing executable documentation. 

The git.R exec is being refactored in #357 and the mailinglist.R exec is being refactored in #385. The ghevents.R, smells.R, and github.R execs need to have their documentation updated to match the new standards we agreed upon.

Here is the proposed documentation updates.

```r
  github_events.R download <project_conf.yml> <token_path>
  github_events.R parse help
```

items.title: Refactor Unit Tests
items.body:
# 1. Pupose
a. The unit tests currently in Kaiaulu are not comprehensive, and do not cover all function categories that should be tested for. Currently test coverage is very sparse across Kaiaulu, with many functions that remain untested. All functions should be tested for in each file, which is something that the current tests do not do. The current tests currently are only organized by file as well, and so should be categorized into different types of tests. The scope of unit test writing should be restricted to the module the group is working on. Tests from other files will be looked at as well, but they take a backseat compared to the current notebook. 

b. I've currently organized Kaiaulu's tests into six categories, which can be organized and reused across multiple different Notebooks. I have created a table categorizing these functions, I plan to create tables for categorizing the types of tests in each notebook the group moves through. The table I have right now serves as a baseline, and I am planning on adding more functions to be tested for as I work through the current Notebooks. 

# 2. Process
a. Add to the existing test files so that it tests all functions available. The code coverage progress and impact of my work can be visualized with codecov, which generates coverage reports from the coverage tool covr. This informs how much code is tested for in Kaiaulu's packages. covr can run both locally or as part of pull request submissions and will show how much is being tested for percentage-wise before new code is merged into Kaiaulu master branch with incomplete coverage. Currently, Kaiaulu has 39.79% of its code tested for. Codecov has the ability to display what lines of code have been tested for already, and I will use that to ensure that I can completely test the Git Log file. 

I was not able to do this completely, and most of what I've done has been testing for the parsers and transforms. The downloaders and refreshers are still not tested for in ```mail.R``` and ```jira.R```. 

### Test Naming
For my tests, I've been using a statement formatted in ```testthat when (function) is given _____, then _____```
I originally started with ```testthat given ____ when ____, then _____``` to follow the format of behavior-driven testing, but ```when``` really only specifies the function being called. To make the format cleaner, I've moved the ```when``` portion of the statement to the front. 
This is something that worked for me when attempting to find a standard way to name tests, but test naming is definitely something that is sort of subjective. The main goal is to follow a single statement format beginning with ```testthat```, which sticks with the conventions of the testthat package. I would recommend future Capstone students to iterate a lot with @carlosparadis regarding test naming and level of abstraction that the test is describing. 

### Transform Test Conventions
For transform tests, developers should try to not call the parser to build the R data table to be fed into the parser. Instead, they should create the R data table using R itself to isolate how the data is being created. If something in the parser breaks, the transform test may fail, even if it was not the fault of the transform function itself. 

### test-graph.R
I've updated some tests for test-graph.R in my Git Log PR. This is because some of the graph functions are called by the transforms to create the respective node and edgelist tables. The transform functions are responsible for filtering out certain nodes from the previous data tables, but the actual logic behind node-edge calculations is called from functions in ```R/graph.R```. 

### Try Catch
I've added a few try catch statements in the parser code to catch errors from the raw data stream from the third party tools. I've added an example of this below. 
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/11abcb41b233f231443783ddf5d13fd5163b0c55/R/git.R#L72-L82

I was originally planning to added try catches to the Git Cmd submodule, but it looks like to me that they return Git status codes and not R errors when they fail, so they wouldn't be caught by ```try catch```. 

# Types of Test
Types of Test | Test Explanation | Examples
| --- | --- | --- |
| Third Party Tools Test(Third Party Tools) | Tests that verify if third party tools are specified, and then test if their -help message is functional | `”testthat given Perceval is specified on tools.yml, when Perceval --help is called, then it returns the help message”` | 
| Data Structure Test(Parsers, Transforms) | Tests that verify functions return the correct data structure | `"testthat when parse_gitlog is given a perceval_path and a ./git folder, then it returns a data table"` |
| Mode/Switch Test(Transforms) | Tests that verify transform functions filter nodes correctly depending on a specified mode | `"testthat when transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network is given a parsed git project and mode, then the type of remaining nodes consist only of those from the mode specified"` | 
| Raw Data Edge Case Test(Parsers) | Tests that feed parsers erroneous/odd data with the intent of breaking its functionality | `"testthat when parse_gitlog is given a ./git folder with a file inside a folder inside another folder, then it will extract the current commit correctly to a data table"` | 
| Error Raising Test(Parsers) | Tests that verify functions will not run when given an invalid input | `"testthat when parse_gitlog is not given .git/, then an error will be raised"` | 
| Expected Behavior Test(All Functions) | Tests that verify a function returned the data it was supposed to. In the context of transforms/graphs, this is correctly preserving node-edge structure. In the context of parsers, this is correctly parsing the data from a file. | `"testthat when bipartite_graph_projection is given a bipartite graph with Author 1 having two connections to File 1 and Author 2 having one connection to File 1, and weight_scheme_function = weight_scheme_sum_edges, and mode = TRUE, then their returned edge is 4"` |

items.title: Refactor Full Config
items.body: # Purpose Currently Kaiaulu uses configuration files to store parameters needed to re-run analyses. This allows users to add new project datasets through creating new .yml (configuration) files and re-running existing notebooks to reuse analysis or write their own. This design choice allows users to avoid duplicating notebooks when changing parameters needed for analyzing a dataset. Instead, users have a single notebook and multiple configuration files per analysis. However, the current Kaiaulu configuration mixes both immutable project data and analysis specific parameters, which if multiple analyses are run at the same time, it would duplicate the same .yml across multiple config files (e.g. project_analysis1.yml, project_analysis2.yml). My goal is to refactor Kaiaulu’s configuration files structure by separating immutable data sections of the .yml file from analysis specific sections of the .yml file so when analyses are run, it will reduce duplication of immutable sections of the .yml file. I.e. instead of project_analysis1.yml, project_analysis2.yml, etc. this work would isolate project.yml from analysis_1.yml, analysis_2.yml. Ideally, analysis.yml can be reused across different project datasets. E.g. analysis_1.yml and analysis_2.yml can also be used through different project_1.yml, project_2.yml etc. This issue shows the overall configuration refactoring, where specific notebook and configuration changes will be sub-issues. If you want to see the starting point, please go to issue #359 . ## Table I made this table to visually show which notebooks are using which configuration .yml files. As well as specific sections in the configuration files that the notebook actually uses to run analyses. # Proposed Changes At the moment, Kaiaulu runs notebooks through parsing project configuration files and calling those parameters through get functions, like this: https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/vignettes/gitlog_showcase.Rmd#L69-L78 After splitting the configuration files into project vs analysis, the notebooks will no longer be parsing through one configuration files but through two; 1 project .yml config file + 1 analysis .yml config file. ``` project <- parse_config("../conf/kaiaulu_immutable.yml") analysis <- parse_config("../conf/analysis1.yml") ``` ## Project vs Analysis What do the split configs look like? What determines immutable vs mutable? Immutable data includes things like repository paths or URLs, things that don't change between analyses. While mutable/analysis specific parameters include things like filters that determine how a specific analysis is run. Here is a diagram that shows this split: ## Tasks - Assess existing /config .yml files and split them into immutable data and analysis specific - Propose/update .yml template so that it can take a project and analysis .yml configuration files (e.g. kaiaulu_immutable.yml + analysis1.yml) - Update implementation in notebooks to support the split configs

The communication focuses on data from Jira. I can grab comments using specific functions such as [`parse_jira`](http://itm0.shidler.hawaii.edu/kaiaulu/reference/parse_jira.html). It parses data obtained from [`download_jira_issues`](http://itm0.shidler.hawaii.edu/kaiaulu/reference/download_jira_issues.html) and returns a named list with two elements (issues, comments) containing the issue table and optionally comments table. Our focus is on the comments table.

An example output of the comments table from `parse_jira` is the following:

items.body:
## Purpose

### Mail
The [mailinglist.R](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/exec/mailinglist.R) executable includes all necessary functionality from the notebook [download_mail.rmd](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/vignettes/download_mail.Rmd).
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/exec/mailinglist.R#L15-L33
The parse works for both pipermail and modmbox since it uses [parse_mbox](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/mail.R#L589]). The only minor change needed is removing the unnecessary and unused input field <end_year_month> in the refresh pipermail command.

### JIRA
Kaiaulu's codebase currently has no executable which includes the functionality showcased in [download_jira_issues.rmd](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/vignettes/download_jira_issues.Rmd). There is a PR #297 which adds a jira exec with the following functionality. 

As is
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/4fef19f3e1950baf76463caa6f0f9b2996d9ec9f/exec/jira.R#L19-L34
The download modmbox command is unnecessary as the mail exec which was created after this PR includes that functionality. This fault was acknowledged in this [comment](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/pull/297/changes#r2483703817).
I think the refresh issues command is the only necessary command. The notebook showcases other downloads such as [download_jira_issues_by_date](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/jira.R#L271), but I don't think it is necessary to have this feature in the executables. Since they are intended to be ran server-side, they are used to process large amounts of data, which means it makes the most sense to just use [refresh_jira_issues](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/jira.R#L406) which will download all issues if none have been downloaded yet. 

## Process

### JIRA
The [JIRA exec](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/4fef19f3e1950baf76463caa6f0f9b2996d9ec9f/exec/jira.R) has a few major flaws. First, it doesn't use the user inputted save path, rather it reads the path from the conf file. This is a simple fix, but I think it makes sense to include the user inputted save path for flexibility and consistency with other execs. 
Secondly, there is no consideration for whether or not authentication is necessary. In the [JIRA notebook](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/vignettes/download_jira_issues.Rmd) it is noted that if you do not need authentication you should comment out the username and password fields. 
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/vignettes/download_jira_issues.Rmd#L154
Since the exec is made to be used in the command line the user will not be able to comment out those lines if authentication is not required. By default we should not require authentication, but when a user needs it, there should be an optional flag --auth which would then require the user to also input their credentials.

Proposed
```R
USAGE:
  jira.R refresh help
  jira.R refresh issues <tools.yml> <project_conf.yml> <save_file_name_path> [(--auth <credentials>)]
  jira.R (-h | --help)
  jira.R --version

DESCRIPTION:
  Provides functions to refresh JIRA issue data with and without comments. Please see
  Kaiaulus README.md for instructions on how to create <tool.yml>
  and <project_conf.yml>.


OPTIONS:
  -h --help     Show this screen.
  --version     Show version.
  --no_auth     Removes requirement for authentication credentials.
```
This shows the functionality to be included, the modmbox downloader is removed and the refresh includes an option for authentication which takes the credentials as input.

items.body:
## Purpose
Kaiaulu currently has the function`github_api_project_commits` to download commits from the GitHub API, but no equivalent function for downloading commit comments. 

This new function is needed to transfer sentiment labels attached to commit comments from the [GHTorrent database](https://web.archive.org/web/20150206005357/http://ghtorrent.org/msr14.html). To map these labels to Kaiaulu-downloaded data, the comment text must be retrieved through Kaiaulu's GitHub API pipeline rather than sourced directly from the static GHTorrent database. The bridge between the sentiment label and the downloaded comment is the **commit comment ID**.

This was identified and discussed in [sailuh/sentiment_github_dataset#1](https://github.com/sailuh/sentiment_github_dataset/issues/1#issuecomment-4014728104).

## Process
Implement a new function called `github_api_project_commit_comments` in `R/github.R` by:
- Referencing the existing `github_api_project_commits` function as a template
- Updating the endpoint to `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/comments` per the [GitHub REST API documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/comments?apiVersion=2022-11-28#list-commit-comments-for-a-repository)
- Updating function parameters to accept `owner`, `repo`, and `token`
- Verifying that returned `comment_id` values match those in GHTorrent's `commit_comments` table

items.title: Implement Productivity Metrics
items.body:
# Purpose
Coming off [the engagement metrics](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/issues/360), we now want to measure developer productivity through commits and lines of code (LOC).

Per Rick's email:
> "Quitting is simply the low end of the engagement scale and rage is the high end of the sentiment/emotion scale. But in this study we are seeking a more nuanced understanding of the relationships. The hypothesis would be that lower sentiment/emotion scores will correlate with lower engagement and lower productivity."

# Process
- Have the productivity metrics for commits and churn be implemented as two functions called 1) `productivity_author_commits` and 2) `productivity_author_churn`
- Understand the input and output of these functions
- Create the function signatures, ensuring relevant parameters are included
- Both functions take into account the 90-day rolling window for its aggregation as we have looked at before with the engagement metrics

## Implementing Commits Productivity
For commits we can use `commit_hash` from the `parse_gitlog` data table to get the unique commits per `author_name_email`. I can then get a simple summation of the overall number of commits. The resulting output would be, for example, the following:
author_name_email | author_datetimetz | author_total_commits
-- | -- | --
Alice Wonderland <<alice@example.com>> | 2024-01-10T11:39:45Z | 5
Bob Smith <<bob@example.com>> | 2024-01-10T11:39:45Z | 3
Charlie Brown <<charlie@example.com>> | 2024-01-05T11:39:45Z | 9

## Implementing Author Churn
I looked at churn metrics that are already implemented including `metric_churn()`, `metric_file_churn()`, `metric_churn_per_commit_per_file()`, etc. and none at first glance take into account per developer churn. 

As such, I can expand upon the existing functions rather than re-do any of them by using [`metric_churn_per_commit_per_file`](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/metric.R#L156) which takes into account the [`metric_churn`](https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/metric.R#L120) function. I see that `metric_churn`
defines churn as the following:
```r
churn <- lines_added + lines_removed
```
So no negative (-) number consideration as Carlos mentions. It treats `lines_added` and `lines_removed` as non-negative counts and defines churn as the summation of the two numbers. As such the example output data table for churn from above would instead look like the following:
author_name_email | author_datetimetz | lines_added | lines_removed | author_churn
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
Alice Wonderland <<alice@example.com>> | 2024-01-01T11:39:45Z | 500 | 50 | 550
Bob Smith <<bob@example.com>> | 2024-04-01T11:39:45Z | 200 | 400 | 600

Using `metric_churn_per_commit_per_file` I can pass in `project_git_log`, which is the data from `parse_gitlog`. Then I can define a variable to hold the developer churn data e.g. `author_churn` and then get the sum of the churn grouped by `author_name_email`. The resulting output would look like the table above.

items.title: Refactor Full Data Schema
items.body: # As-is # 1. Purpose ## 1. Standardizing Data Entities Context: Based on Issue #226, the Kāiaulu architecture was partially planned and partially built as features were added incrementally without following a centralized plan. This resulted in an "accidental architecture" where identical data entities are represented by inconsistent column names and values across different tables. Impact: This inconsistency makes it difficult to perform inner joins across tables. Without standardized keys, the user has to guess from the notebook content what in each notebook can be inner joined to other tables. Resolution: Establish a standardized naming convention and data representation for all tables that are relevant for Kaiaulu users, ensuring every primary and foreign key is uniform across the entire environment. ## 2. Establishing a Formal Schema Context: Due to Kāiaulu’s organic growth, there was no clear vision for how data saved by one notebook links to another, causing technical debt to accrue in the schema. Impact: Users are forced to guess relationships or read through entire notebooks to understand how datasets connect, resulting in a lack of transparency and unindexed data. Resolution: Represent the tables and columns currently residing in Notebooks as formal entities within MySQL Workbench (.mwb). This provides an explicit, self-documenting data model where related columns share the exact same name and can be joined reliably. ## 3. Enforcing Future Consistency Context: Even with a formal schema in place, new developers may inadvertently introduce inconsistent naming or data structures when creating new notebooks, which would eventually undo these architectural improvements. Impact: Without a "guardrail," the effort to clean up the architecture will deteriorate over time, leading back to a fragmented and unmaintainable system. Resolution: Develop a set of R functions within R/io.R to define a strict code API for data storage. This programmatic layer ensures that any data saved by a notebook adheres to the defined schema, preventing "accidental" naming deviations in the future. # 2. Process The process will use the previous, incomplete efforts from Issue #226 as a baseline, but will prioritize the current state of the code as the source of truth. ### 1. Purpose
Codecov is a tool currently in Kaiaulu that provides metrics and insights into the coverage reports created by the ```covr``` package, which tracks displays total code coverage from the tests created with the ```testthat``` package. Codecov operates with both a global level ```yml``` file and a repository level ```yml``` file. Both these ```yml``` files allow Codecov to do things like comment on PRs, display coverage changes from PRs, enforce test coverage requirements in PRs, and distinguish between patch test coverage and repo-wide test coverage. The global ```yml``` file is what Codecov defaults to using across the whole organization. In this case, all projects under Sailuh, including Kaiaulu should be defaulting to this file. The repo level ```yml``` would take priority over the global ```yml```, but it doesn't currently exist in Kaiaulu. 

### 2. Process
For that reason, I would like to create a new ```codecov.yml``` file in the Kaiaulu repository to enforce better testing coverage standards on PRs. I would also configure it to display useful information in its PR comments, and take a look at its flag management system. In order to do this, I will iterate with @carlosparadis in order to find the best way to utilize Codecov for Kaiaulu.

items.title: Define Consistent Transform Interfaces and Graph Abstractions Across Kaiaulu Pipelines
items.body: # Purpose This project standardizes how Kaiaulu's data transform pipelines produce network outputs. Kaiaulu supports multiple data sources including Git, Jira, GitHub, mailing lists, and source code analysis tools. Before this work, the transform functions across these pipelines had evolved independently. They did not produce comparable outputs, they used inconsistent internal structures, and downstream analysis code often had to work around these differences at the notebook level. The work done here defines a shared pipeline contract across all data sources: ``` parse_* ↓ transform_*_to_network ↓ model_(unimodal|multimodal)_graph ↓ projections / exports / metrics ``` Every transform function now produces a typed graph object by building an explicit nodes table and edgelist table and passing them to the appropriate `model_*` constructor. `model_unimodal_graph` is used when all nodes are the same type; `model_multimodal_graph` is used when nodes are of two or more distinct types, with `is_bipartite = TRUE` for bipartite graphs. This means downstream functions like projections, DSM export, and analysis metrics can operate on any graph object without needing to know which pipeline produced it. # Process ## Git Log, Depends, Understand As I began Milestone 1, I wanted to confirm my understanding of the code layout referenced in prior discussions. While `graph.R` exists in the `R` folder, `network.R` does not appear to exist in the current repository. Based on inspection of the codebase, it appears that functionality previously associated with `network.R` has been split across source-specific files such as `git.R`, `jira.R`, `github.R`, `mail.R`, and parts of `src.R`. In particular, the transform functions for the Depends and Understand pipelines appear to live in `src.R`. To understand current behavior, I reviewed existing code, vignettes, and performed hands-on testing of the `Git`, `Depends`, and `Understand` pipelines. Based on this work, I created a diagram representing how each pipeline currently operates. The diagram shows where external CLI tools are used, how data is transformed in R, and where each pipeline terminates. The diagram reflects observed behavior rather than intended or future architecture. Through this review, several cross-pipeline inconsistencies were identified. The `Git` pipeline constructs graph objects using `model_directed_graph()` and then applies projections and weighting, while the `Depends` and `Understand` pipelines stop at node and edge list outputs and do not construct graph objects inside Kaiaulu. Because of this, outputs from different pipelines are not directly interchangeable. During testing of the `Depends` pipeline, schema and naming issues were encountered. In one case, `parse_dependencies()` produced a nodes table with a name column, while `transform_dependencies_to_network()` expected a filepath column, causing the transform to fail unless the column was manually renamed. A separate issue was observed where the Depends CLI produced a JSON file with a `-file.json` suffix instead of the expected filename, leading Kaiaulu to fail when parsing the output despite successful CLI execution. Differences in how edge weights are handled were also observed. The weight_types parameter has different meanings across pipelines. In the `Depends` pipeline, it determines which dependency-type columns are summed to produce a numeric edge weight. In the `Understand` pipeline, it only filters dependency kinds without computing numeric weights. In the `Git` pipeline, weighting is applied later, after graph construction. As a result, edge weights are not directly comparable across data sources. Finally, while reviewing and testing the `Git` entity-based temporal transforms, I observed that column renaming behavior differs depending on the mode being used, which makes transform behavior harder to reason about at the API level. ## GitHub, Jira, Mail As a continuation of M1, I reviewed the `GitHub`, `Jira`, and `Mail` transform pipelines to understand how data moves from raw artifacts into structured outputs in the current Kaiaulu codebase. This review follows the same process I used earlier for the `Git`, `Depends`, and `Understand` pipelines. The goal was to document how the pipelines actually behave today, identify where they stop, and note any issues or inconsistencies I encountered while tracing the code. I focused on the boundaries of each pipeline rather than internal implementation details. For the `GitHub` pipeline, I examined the download functions that retrieve issues, pull requests, comments, and commits from the GitHub API. These functions operate independently and write raw JSON files to disk. All parsing and transformation logic is handled by the function `parse_github_replies`, which reads the downloaded JSON artifacts and normalizes them into a single replies table. This function combines parsing and transformation into one step and relies on several helper functions internally. There are no intermediate tables exposed, and the pipeline stops once the replies table is produced. One issue I noted is that the reply schema is assumed implicitly across helper functions, and there is no clear separation between parsing raw data and applying semantic transformations. For the Jira pipeline, the structure is more clearly separated. Raw issue data is downloaded using `download_jira_issues`, after which `parse_jira` converts the JSON files into issues and comments tables. A second function, `parse_jira_replies`, then transforms those tables into a normalized replies table. The pipeline stops at that point. Compared to `GitHub` and `Mail`, `Jira` is the only pipeline that exposes intermediate tables. While this makes the transformation steps easier to follow, the replies transformation assumes that issues and comments are complete and correctly linked, and there is no explicit validation of those assumptions in the code. The `Mail` pipeline follows a different pattern. Mailing list archives are downloaded as mbox files and then processed by the function `parse_mbox`. This function calls Perceval to extract message data and immediately normalizes it into a replies table. Parsing and transformation are fully combined, and the pipeline ends after the replies table is created. I noticed that much of the important logic, such as reply construction and identity handling, is implemented in helper functions that are not visible at the pipeline level. The pipeline also depends heavily on Perceval, but error handling and failure cases are not clearly surfaced. Across all three pipelines, the final output is a replies table, and none of the pipelines perform graph construction or projection. Even though the replies table is compatible with later graph modeling steps, those steps are not part of these pipelines as implemented. Any use of graph utilities happens outside of these pipelines. Another issue I observed is that refresh functions exist for extraction in each pipeline, but they operate independently and are not integrated into the main transformation flow, which makes them easy to miss when reading the pipeline logic. Overall, the `GitHub`, `Jira`, and `Mail` pipelines function as ingestion and normalization pipelines. They successfully standardize different data sources into a common replies format, but they do so with inconsistent structure and implicit assumptions. Documenting these behaviors and boundaries is important so that downstream workflows do not assume functionality that is not actually present in the current implementation. ## Experiment: Applying `model_directed_graph()` to Depends As part of Milestone 1, I ran an experiment applying `model_directed_graph()` to the output of the Depends pipeline. The objective was to determine whether Depends could be elevated to the same abstraction layer as GitLog and to identify what structural changes would be required. The Depends pipeline currently proceeds as follows: 1. `parse_dependencies()` invokes the Depends CLI and parses its JSON output into a structured object containing file-level nodes and a dependency-type edgelist. 2. `transform_dependencies_to_network()` collapses the dependency-type matrix into a weighted file-to-file network, producing `nodes(name, color)` and `edgelist(from, to, weight)`. At this point, the pipeline terminates and returns a weighted network representation. In the experiment, I applied `model_directed_graph()` directly to the weighted edgelist returned by `transform_dependencies_to_network()`. This produced a `directed_graph` object containing: - `nodes(name, type, color)` - `edgelist(from, to, weight)` Structurally, this matches the abstraction level produced by the GitLog pipeline. ### Comparison: GitLog vs Depends Comparing the revised Depends pipeline to GitLog reveals an important architectural difference. In the GitLog pipeline, graph abstraction is constructed inside the transform functions themselves. For example, `transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network()` generates an edgelist and immediately calls `model_directed_graph()`, after which projections and weighting logic are applied to the resulting graph object. The Git pipeline therefore transitions into the graph abstraction layer during transformation. In contrast, the current Depends pipeline produces a weighted network list but does not enter the graph abstraction layer unless `model_directed_graph()` is applied explicitly afterward. The experiment demonstrates that Depends can cleanly align with GitLog once this additional step is introduced. There is no structural difference in the inputs or outputs required by `model_directed_graph()` between the two pipelines. In both cases, the function expects an edgelist with `from`, `to`, and optionally `weight`. However, the semantic meaning differs. In GitLog, edges often represent developer-to-file relationships and may involve bipartite or temporal structures. In Depends, edges represent static file-to-file dependencies. The abstraction layer is therefore consistent, even though the domain semantics differ. ### Constructing a `model_undirected_graph()` Abstraction During this comparison, it also became clear that Kaiaulu currently assumes directed graphs as the default abstraction. While this is appropriate for many pipelines (such as commit or dependency flows), some data sources are conceptually symmetric. For example, co-change networks, co-authorship networks, or certain projections derived from GitHub, Jira, or mail replies may be better represented as undirected graphs. A `model_undirected_graph()` function could be constructed analogously to `model_directed_graph()`, but would normalize edge directionality before building the graph abstraction. Conceptually, this would involve: 1. Taking an edgelist with `from`, `to`, and optional `weight`. 2. Sorting or canonicalizing node pairs so that `(A, B)` and `(B, A)` are treated as the same edge. 3. Aggregating duplicate edges by summing weights where appropriate. 4. Constructing a graph object flagged as undirected. The resulting abstraction would maintain the same standardized schema for nodes and edges but remove directionality from the representation. This would allow pipelines that naturally produce symmetric relationships to converge to the same graph abstraction contract without artificially imposing direction. Introducing `model_undirected_graph()` would further support Milestone 2's goal of defining consistent transform interfaces. Instead of each pipeline implicitly deciding whether it is directed or undirected, the abstraction choice would be explicit and standardized at the graph-construction layer. ### Implications for Standardization The experiment shows that the Depends pipeline can be aligned with GitLog at the graph abstraction level. Once `model_directed_graph()` is applied, both pipelines produce structurally consistent `directed_graph` objects with compatible node and edge schemas. The remaining differences are semantic rather than structural. Introducing both `model_directed_graph()` and a potential `model_undirected_graph()` abstraction would allow all pipelines to converge on a shared contract: ``` parse_* ↓ transform_*_to_network ↓ model_(directed|undirected)_graph ↓ projections / exports / metrics ``` Downstream projections, exports such as DSM, and analysis workflows could then operate uniformly on graph objects rather than pipeline-specific list structures. This experiment, therefore, not only validates the feasibility of standardizing Depends but also suggests a broader architectural improvement for Kaiaulu's graph modeling layer moving forward. ## Transform Function Standardization The `transform_*` functions across Kaiaulu were refactored to follow a consistent pattern. Each function now builds an explicit nodes table and an explicit edgelist table, then passes them to the appropriate constructor before returning. Previously, some functions returned plain lists with no class, used outdated constructor parameters, or left graph construction to the caller. The two constructors are `model_unimodal_graph`, for graphs where all nodes are the same type (e.g. file-file dependency networks), and `model_multimodal_graph`, for graphs where nodes are of two or more distinct types (e.g. author-file or author-thread networks). Bipartite graphs use `model_multimodal_graph` with `is_bipartite = TRUE`. In both cases, the transform is responsible for building the nodes and edgelist tables before calling the constructor — the constructor only wraps them and assigns the S3 class. The standardized pattern is: ```r nodes <- data.table(name = ..., type = ..., color = ...) edgelist <- data.table(from = ..., to = ..., weight = ..., direction = ...) graph <- model_unimodal_graph(nodes, edgelist, direction = ...) return(graph) ``` Downstream functions such as `graph_to_dsmj`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, and `temporal_graph_projection` use S3 dispatch on the graph class. Because every transform function now returns a properly typed graph object, these functions dispatch correctly without any caller-side workarounds. ### Transform Functions The following checklist shows the refactoring status of all `transform_*` functions across the codebase: **R/git.R** - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network` - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network` - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_entity_bipartite_network` - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_entity_temporal_network` - [x] `transform_commit_message_id_to_network` - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_heterogeneous_network` **R/reply.R** - [x] `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network` (covers GitHub, Jira, and Mail pipelines) **R/src.R** - [x] `transform_understand_dependencies_to_network` - [x] `transform_dependencies_to_network` - [x] `transform_r_dependencies_to_network` **R/dv8.R** - [x] `transform_dependencies_to_sdsmj` - [x] `transform_gitlog_to_hdsmj` - [x] `transform_temporal_gitlog_to_adsmj` **R/vulnerabilities.R** - [x] `transform_cve_cwe_file_to_network` ### Affected Notebooks #### All Image Comparisons showcase Master Branch (left/top) vs Dev Branch (right/bottom) - [x] `vignettes/gitlog_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network` - [x] `vignettes/gitlog_entity_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_entity_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_gitlog_to_entity_temporal_network` - [x] `vignettes/community_detection_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network`, `transform_dependencies_to_network` The two branches assign different **integer IDs** to nodes before running OSLOM. OSLOM uses those IDs internally with a random seed. Same seed + different IDs = different community assignments and colors. The ID assignment comes from `mapping_names <- unique(c(edgelist$from, edgelist$to))` in `community_oslom` — the order nodes appear in that list determines their ID. Because the S3 refactoring changed how the node table is built internally (all-from-nodes first then all-to-nodes, vs interleaved), the projected edgelist has a slightly different row order, which changes the `mapping_names` sequence, which changes the IDs fed to OSLOM. **The weights are correct. The graph structure is correct. Only the node ID ordering going into OSLOM differs**, causing different (but equally valid) community partitions. - [x] `vignettes/social_smell_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network` - [x] `vignettes/issue_social_smell_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network`, `transform_commit_message_id_to_network` - [x] `vignettes/causal_flaws.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network`, `transform_gitlog_to_hdsmj`, `transform_dependencies_to_sdsmj` - [x] `vignettes/motif_analysis.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_bipartite_network`, `bipartite_graph_projection`, `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network`, `transform_r_dependencies_to_network` The `motif_analysis.Rmd` square motif section parses `../R` (the kaiaulu R source folder itself) to build a file dependency network. Because the dev branch adds new R source files and functions as part of issue #361, the parsed file dependency graph has one more edge than master's (30 vs 29). This changes the combined `file_git_reply_network` edge count (128 vs 127), which causes `visIgraph(randomSeed=1)` to produce a different force-directed layout — the same seed initializes differently when the graph topology changes. The layout difference is expected and correct. It reflects that the dev branch contains additional R code, not a regression in the network construction logic. - [x] `vignettes/reply_communication_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_reply_to_bipartite_network` - [x] `vignettes/gitlog_vulnerabilities_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_commit_message_id_to_network`, `transform_cve_cwe_file_to_network` - [x] `vignettes/bug_count.Rmd` — `transform_commit_message_id_to_network` - [x] `vignettes/dv8_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_gitlog_to_hdsmj`, `transform_dependencies_to_sdsmj` - [x] `vignettes/depends_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_dependencies_to_network` - [x] `vignettes/understand_showcase.Rmd` — `transform_understand_dependencies_to_network` - [x] `vignettes/kaiaulu_architecture.Rmd` — `transform_r_dependencies_to_network` Differences found in these images are due to the Kaiaulu Architecture notebook running on the current branch of Kaiaulu. The development branch includes new functions, causing differences in the notebook from Master to Dev. ## Graph to DSMJ Export File Test [kaiaulu-bdsm.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26815876/kaiaulu-bdsm.json) ## Tool Comparisons **NetworkX, SNAP, and igraph** NetworkX and SNAP both handle data loading and graph construction in a single step where you pass in raw data and get a graph object back with no separation between the two stages. igraph follows the same pattern in R where constructor functions like `graph_from_data_frame()` consume a data frame and return a graph object all at once. igraph is the closest in similarity to Kaiaulu since it also uses R's S3 class system. The key difference is that igraph uses a single `igraph` class for all graph types and stores properties like directionality and bipartite membership as flags and vertex attributes on the same object. Kaiaulu instead uses separate S3 classes (`bipartite_graph`, `heterogeneous_graph`, `directed_graph`) which makes the graph type explicit and allows S3 dispatch to automatically route projection and export functions to the correct method. igraph supports bipartite graphs as a first-class feature but treats heterogeneous graphs by convention only where users manually set a type attribute and filter nodes and edges themselves. **git2net and coronet** These are the most direct comparisons since both libraries transform software engineering data into networks. git2net separates parsing from graph construction by persisting all extracted git data to a SQLite database first since mining a repository is expensive and should only be done once. coronet takes a more structured approach with a four-part architecture where configuration, data loading, network configuration, and graph construction are each handled by separate classes. Kaiaulu currently sits between these two approaches. The transform functions do separate data preparation from graph construction but there is no persistent intermediate layer like a database or a formal data class connecting the two. The advantage of this is simplicity. Where Kaiaulu stands apart from both libraries is heterogeneous graph support. Neither git2net nor coronet provides a native heterogeneous graph type. Kaiaulu's `model_heterogeneous_graph` with explicit string node and edge types is a more expressive abstraction for multi-type networks that neither library currently offers. **Quanteda** Quanteda is the closest in similarity to where Kaiaulu's S3 system is heading. Quanteda defines a strict pipeline of S3 classes (`corpus` → `tokens` → `dfm`) where each class has its own dedicated set of functions following a `class_verb()` naming convention. This makes the API predictable and self-documenting since users always know what functions exist for a given object type. The core takeaway is that consistent naming conventions and per-class function sets can make a system intuitive and maintainable without requiring more complex class systems like S4 or R6. Kaiaulu's `model_*` constructors and `bipartite_graph_projection` S3 generic are already moving in this direction. **Codeface** Codeface stores everything in a MySQL database and runs from the command line with no library API. Any analysis means querying MySQL directly or using a Shiny web app. It has not been maintained since 2022. The big takeaway is that a heavy setup creates a barrier. Having to install Vagrant, MySQL, and a web server just to run an analysis is a lot, and Kaiaulu avoids all of that by keeping things in memory. **SmartSHARK** SmartSHARK pushes separation of concerns the furthest out of all of these tools. Each data source is its own separate command-line tool, and they all write into a shared MongoDB database using a shared data format called pycoSHARK. The way SmartSHARK splits things by data source at the repo level is basically what Kaiaulu does at the file level with R/jira.R, R/github.R, and so on. It shows that the separation is the right call. It also shows what happens when you take it too far. Setting up a full SmartSHARK environment means deploying MongoDB, a Django web server, a background worker, and configuring every plugin on its own, which is way more than most researchers want to deal with. **PyDriller** PyDriller is a Python library that gives you a clean API for reading Git repositories. You create a Repository object, iterate over commits, and each commit gives you file changes, diffs, blame data, and complexity numbers. There is no command-line tool, and nothing gets saved to disk. The API is simple and easy to use. The downside is that every time you run an analysis, it has to re-read the whole repository, which is slow for big projects. Compared to Kaiaulu wrapping Perceval as a command-line tool, PyDriller shows what it looks like to build a proper library for Git data. Kaiaulu goes through Perceval, which adds a step, but it covers a lot more data sources than just Git. **Perceval** Perceval supports over 40 different data sources, including Git, GitHub, Jira, Bugzilla, mailing lists, and CI systems. It outputs one JSON object per item and streams it to the console. Kaiaulu uses it as a command-line dependency for parse_gitlog, so Kaiaulu runs the perceval program and reads its output rather than using it as a library. Perceval choosing to be a command-line tool instead of a library is the opposite of what PyDriller does. For Kaiaulu, this means the Git data collection part is stable and does not need to be maintained, but it also means it cannot be changed from within R. It is a clean split between collecting data and analyzing it, at the cost of needing Perceval installed.

# Purpose
## Engagement Communication
```r
engagement_communication <- function(datetimetz, user_name_email, quit_lag = 90)
```
The `engagement_communication` function checks the author (`user_name_email`) and applies the rolling window (`quit_lag`) of 90 days. For each window of 90 days, the function counts (using a function that counts so in data.table the .N will likely be needed) up the number of comments for each author and outputs that as a table as shown above.

## Engagement Sentiment
```r
engagement_sentiment <- function(datetimetz, user_name_email, polarity, quit_lag = 90, aggregate_func)
```
For the `engagement_sentiment`, it re-uses much of the logic as `engagement_communication` but it will instead apply an aggregate function to the sentiment (`polarity`) for each 90 day window (`quit_lag`) from the author (`user_name_email`). This way, we can see for each window, what an author's overall sentiment was. We are still taking into account Samantha's data, so then the string values that her data has e.g. `positive`, `neutral`, `negative` would have to be converted to the numerical representation first to then apply an aggregate function for the overall polarity for each author's window. The `aggregate_func` is passed as parameter. In R, you can pass both variables and function definitions as parameters. items.body:
## 1. Purpose
Before Kaiaulu had configuration files, in order to run analysis, you had to copy and paste notebooks for each projects. Then edit a few lines to rerun the analysis. This is bad in terms of scalability and increases maintenance over time. 

Kaiaulu then addressed this problem by using configuration files. You no longer have duplicated notebooks but a single notebook and multiple configuration files. This allows people to add new projects through editing .yml file and not a new notebook. As well as fixing bugs and adding new features by editing a single notebook.

However, the current Kaiaulu configuration design mixes two concerns in the same .yml file:
1) Immutable project data (ex. log url, repo paths)
2) Analysis specific (ex. filters)

This means if multiple analyses are being run for the same project, you would have to duplicate the same content across multiple configuration files even though the data isn't changing. 

My goal for the first milestone would be to assess the .yml files in the config folder and determine which sections of each .yml are imutable, propose an updated .yml template, and update Kaiaulu's implementation one notebook at a time.

My goal for the second milestone is based on user case A. scenario where there will be a lot of projects but few analyses being used. After M1, now project configs can be seen as datasets. M2 will explore how Kaiaulu can take advantage of looking at configs as data and generate summaries across many different projects. These summaries will help users understand and analyze these large amount of projects (e.g. which projects have specific data sources and how analysis parameters may vary).

My goal for the third milestone is based on user case B. opposite of user case A. now we have a small number of projects but a lot of analyses. After M1, analysis configs should be reusable so M3 is about proposing ideas what Kaiaulu can do with them. Will further discuss on details after M1 is complete.

## 2. Process
### M1
My first step would be to go through the current existing /conf .yml files and identify which ones are immutable data and analysis specific. 
Ex. using the tse_apex.yml you provided below
Immutable data:
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/conf/tse_apex.yml#L31-L44
Typically project and version_control are considered immutable data as the website and what the project is about typically don't change per analysis or even through multiple analyses. 

Analysis specific:
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/conf/tse_apex.yml#L119-L131
Filters should belong in analysis specific as can differ through multiple analyses.

After classification, I will split the immutable data and analysis specific into different .yml files. We don't want to make configs for everything as it would be too much for users to go through but also not have it in one big config file. So I propose we should keep a immutable data config for each project but have a reusable shared analyses per notebook. I will jointly discuss with my team the purpose of the notebook, as well as my responsibility to work on the config refactor work while coordinating with the team.

## 3. Task List
### M1
Part 1: Assessing config

- [x] Identify existing .yml files for which ones are immutable data
- [x] Identify existing .yml files for which ones are analysis specific
- [x] Identify existing .yml files that are different from current template and classify them as outdated (to either update vs. ignore)

Part 2: Update .yml template
- [x] Go through each notebook, identify notebook specific configurations
- [x] Propose a data config structure/template
- [x] Propose a analysis config structure/template

Part 3:  Update implementation
- [ ] Update notebooks to support split configs

## Next Step
After finishing up gitlog notebook, will move on to working on depends/scitools notebook. Making sure that those notebooks can also support split configs. Also another goal is to start working through M2 & M3 which is further explained in issue #366 .

items.body:
## 1. Purpose
The executables in Kaiaulu currently have limited capabilities. There are only 5 files vs the 20+ notebooks. Exec files should include logical functionality which may have some overlap with the notebooks. Integrate necessary functions from notebooks but exclude unnecessary things such as graphing which doesn't make sense for the exec files to do. There are also certain functionalities that need to be added to executables which are not in the notebooks. For example, gitlog_showcase.rmd includes graphs which show the authors that edited each file. This cannot be used directly in an executable because we don't want to make graphs, but we may still need to get this information from the exec, so we can represent it differently for the exec.

## 2. Process
Iterate through notebooks and make sure there is an associated executable file which has any necessary functionality whether it is from the notebook or others that you think are necessary.
Think about what functions/analysis you would like to have in the execs for easier data access.

Executables need to be updated side by side with notebooks and config files, so I will work with the Kaiaulu architecture group to update modules and notebooks one by one, beginning with the Git module and Git Log notebook.

## 3. Task List
Currently all the executable is capable of is outputting the commit log of a repo. 

- [ ] Update executable description to make it more obvious what the file does since "tabulate" is a bit confusing https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/exec/git.R#L20-L23
- [ ] Add parse_git_blame to executable. This function parses the git blame of a file. It may be useful to be able to run this on all files of certain types in a repo. I think this is useful data for the executable.
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/git.R#L151-L160
- [ ] Add parse_gitlog_entity to executable. This function builds on the parse git log function to include the type of code authors change, such as functions, classes, and methods. This seems like an important function for the purposes of the executable, although the function description states it can take hours to run.
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/git.R#L289-L296


- [ ] The transform_gitlog_to_temporal_network function provides useful analyses about the collaboration of authors in a repo. The issue is that the function returns a graph of the collaboration network. For the purposes of the executable we would want a csv of authors and edgeweights. Additionally I am unsure that this is the right type of functionality for the executable, should the executable be performing analysis or just parsing data?
https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/5bbdbb2834df02971e604cb20207f2d25e3acc56/R/git.R#L814-L820

### 1. Pupose a. The unit tests currently in Kaiaulu are not comprehensive, and do not cover all function categories that should be tested for. Currently 9 R test files exist while there are 17 modules, each with functions that should be tested for. All functions should be tested for in each file as well, which is something that the current tests do not do. For example, test-mail.R only tests the function parse_mbox() even though there are other functions that pertain to mail, like download_mod_mbox and make_mbox_reply. The same is true in test-jira.R, where only parse_jira is tested for, and no other functions. The scope of unit test writing should be restricted to the module the group is working on. Currently, that is Git Log. Tests from other files will be looked at as well, but they take a backseat compared to the current notebook. b. I've currently organized Kaiaulu's tests into three categories, which can be organized and reused across multiple different Notebooks. These current categories are the Fake Data Generation/Foundational Tests, Path Tests, and Behavior Tests. Fake Data Generation/Foundational Tests have the sole purpose of testing the fake data generation functions in Kaiaulu. They are foundational because without ensuring that the fake data generation functions work correctly, all tests that rely on them would be unreliable. Path Tests are easily replicable, and are responsible for testing the response of functions when given correct or incorrect paths/inputs. Behavior Tests test what functions actually do given certain inputs, and that they give the correct output. I have created a table categorizing these functions, I plan to create tables for categorizing the types of tests in each notebook the group moves through. If current tests have potential to be used elsewhere in other test files, I would take note of it as well. Test priority would be assessed through the amount of times a function is called in its Git Notebooks. For the Git Log module, the Notebooks we are currently moving through are ```gitlog_showcase.Rmd``` and ```gitlog_entity_showcase.Rmd```. Although the functions being used in the notebooks take priority, I would be creating tests for all functions in R/git.R to supplement Notebook overall health. The table I have right not serves as a baseline, and I am planning on adding more functions to be tested for as I work through the current Notebooks. I've also broken up the R/example.R functions from those in Git Log, because testing for them is completely different. ### 2. Process a. Add to the existing Git Log file so that it tests all functions available. The code coverage progress and impact of my work can be visualized with codecov, which is a coverage tool that informs how much code is tested for in Kaiaulu's packages. Codecov can run both locally or as part of pull request submissions and will show how much is being tested for percentage-wise before new code is merged into Kaiaulu master branch with incomplete coverage. Currently, Kaiaulu has 39.79% of its code tested for. Codecov has the ability to display what lines of code have been tested for already, and I will use that to ensure that I can completely test the Git Log file. b.
